cards.title: European Union (Withdrawal) Act main Motion (Prime Minister)
cards.headline: Approve the negotiated Brexit divorce treaty and the outline of the future relationship: leave the EU on 29 March 2019 with citizens' rights guaranteed, a £39 billion settlement, business rules frozen until the end of 2020 — and a customs 'backstop' the UK cannot leave without the EU's agreement.
cards.source_brief:
Two and a half years after the referendum, this is the full divorce package: a legally binding treaty of nearly 600 pages settling the money, citizens and the Irish border, paired with a short, non-binding sketch of the future trade relationship. Approve it and the UK leaves on time and in order, with almost two more years to negotiate what comes next. The price is paying the bill before the future is written — and an insurance clause with no exit door of its own.

- **What you get:** a standstill until the **end of 2020** — travel, trade and daily life unchanged while the future deal is negotiated — guaranteed rights for the **3 million+** EU citizens in the UK and **~1 million** Britons in the EU, and an agreed financial settlement of about **£39 billion**.
- **The catch — the backstop:** if no trade deal is ready when the standstill ends, the whole UK stays locked in EU customs rules, with Northern Ireland following extra EU rules on goods, **until both sides agree** to end it. The UK cannot walk out of it alone.
- **The blank page:** the future relationship — trade, security, fishing — is only a **26-page wish list** with no legal force. The £39 billion is committed before anyone knows what the final relationship looks like.
- **The handle:** an orderly, predictable exit now, versus signing an open-ended customs tie whose key is held jointly in London **and** Brussels — certainty today against leverage tomorrow.
cards.deep_facts:
- The motion is moved under **section 13(1)(b)** of the EU (Withdrawal) Act 2018: the treaty cannot be ratified unless the Commons approves both the negotiated withdrawal agreement and the framework for the future relationship (EU (Withdrawal) Act 2018; Hansard, 15 Jan 2019).
- The withdrawal agreement was endorsed by EU27 leaders on **25 November 2018** and laid before the House on **26 November 2018**, together with the Political Declaration (Hansard, 15 Jan 2019; European Council, 25 Nov 2018).
- **Financial settlement:** the treaty fixes a formula, not a figure, covering commitments made as a member; the Government's estimate is **£35–39 billion**, paid over many years (HM Treasury estimate; Institute for Government).
- **Transition:** EU law continues to apply to the UK until **31 December 2020**; the period can be extended **once**, by joint UK–EU decision taken before **1 July 2020** (Withdrawal Agreement, Arts. 126–132). During it the UK leaves the EU's institutions but follows its rules, including new ones.
- **Citizens:** EU citizens lawfully resident in the UK and UK nationals lawfully resident in the EU at the end of the transition keep residence, work and healthcare rights; **five years'** residence brings a permanent right to stay (Withdrawal Agreement, Part Two).
- **Backstop:** the Protocol on Ireland/Northern Ireland establishes a **single EU–UK customs territory** from the end of the transition "unless and until" a future agreement supersedes it, with Northern Ireland additionally aligned to single-market rules for goods; ending it requires a **joint** UK–EU decision that it is "no longer necessary" (Protocol, Arts. 6 and 20).
- The Attorney General's published advice states that in international law the Protocol "would endure indefinitely" until superseded by a subsequent agreement (Attorney General's advice of 13 Nov 2018, published 5 Dec 2018).
- The **Political Declaration** is expressly not legally binding; it sets objectives for an "ambitious, broad, deep and flexible partnership" to be negotiated only after exit (Political Declaration, 25 Nov 2018, 26 pp.).
- Exit day in law at the time of the vote: **29 March 2019**, two years after the UK's Article 50 notification — the treaty clause that starts a two-year countdown to leaving (EU (Withdrawal) Act 2018, s20).
cards.deep_lectura:
**Analyst read** *(inference — not stated verbatim in the record)*
- The package's architecture is a sequencing of leverage: everything the EU most needed (money, citizens, the Irish border) is in the binding treaty; everything the UK most wanted (the future trade deal) sits in the non-binding declaration. The day the treaty is ratified, a fresh negotiating clock starts ticking — with the £39 billion already committed.
- The backstop functions less as a border fix than as a floor under all future negotiation: any future deal must keep the Irish border at least as open as the backstop does, which quietly excludes the more distant trading models before those talks even begin.
- A 21-month transition is shorter than any modern trade negotiation has ever taken; the realistic end-states are extension, the backstop, or a thin deal — a choice the text never states but its calendar makes.
- The treaty's dispute system sends questions of EU law to the EU's own court, so for the backstop's duration the referee and one of the teams share a shirt — defensible legally, combustible politically.

cards.title: Section 13(1)(b) of the European Union (Withdrawal) Act main motion
cards.headline: Approve the Brexit deal as a five-document package: the divorce treaty (£39 billion settlement, citizens' rights, standstill to end-2020, the customs backstop) together with legally binding instruments signed in Strasbourg guaranteeing the EU cannot deliberately trap the UK in the backstop.
cards.source_brief:
The package on the table pairs the divorce treaty with documents signed in Strasbourg on the eve of this vote: a joint instrument with treaty-level legal force on the backstop — the insurance clause keeping the UK in EU customs rules until both sides agree a replacement — plus a UK declaration and a joint statement on fast-tracking its replacement. The treaty's text is untouched; what changes is how it must be read. The whole question is what those assurances are worth.

- **The treaty:** an orderly exit — about **£39 billion** settled, rights guaranteed for **3 million+** EU citizens in the UK and **~1 million** Britons in the EU, business rules frozen to **end-2020** while the future relationship is negotiated.
- **The new assurances:** with binding force, deliberately keeping the UK in the backstop would breach the deal; the UK could then go to arbitration and **suspend** the backstop. Both sides also commit to work to replace it with 'alternative arrangements' by **December 2020**.
- **What they don't do:** the Government's own chief legal adviser concluded the core risk is **unchanged** — if talks simply deadlock with nobody acting in bad faith, the UK still has **no lawful way out of the backstop on its own**.
- **The handle:** certainty plus sharpened legal teeth against bad faith — or the same open-ended customs tie if negotiations merely stall, with £39 billion committed to a future still written in pencil.
cards.deep_facts:
- The motion, under **section 13(1)(b)** of the EU (Withdrawal) Act 2018, asks the House to approve **five documents**: the negotiated withdrawal agreement; the framework for the future relationship (the Political Declaration); a **joint, legally binding instrument** on the agreement and the Protocol on Ireland/Northern Ireland; a **joint statement** supplementing the Political Declaration; and a **unilateral declaration** by the UK on the Protocol (Hansard, 12 Mar 2019).
- The joint instrument and unilateral declaration were concluded in **Strasbourg on 11 March 2019**; under Article 31 of the Vienna Convention they take effect as an authentic, binding interpretation of the treaty — they do not amend its text (Attorney General's legal opinion, 12 Mar 2019, paras 1–3).
- **Joint instrument:** a "systematic refusal to take into consideration adverse proposals or interests" would breach the good-faith/best-endeavours duties; replacing the Protocol is to be treated as a priority, with efforts "redoubled" if no replacement is concluded within a year of withdrawal; a dedicated negotiating track on **alternative arrangements** (customs cooperation, facilitative technologies) aims to establish them **by 31 December 2020**; a replacement "is not required to replicate" the Protocol (Joint instrument, paras 4–10; AG opinion, paras 5–8).
- **Enforcement:** if the UK demonstrated the EU was acting to apply the Protocol indefinitely, the EU could not dispute a breach of good faith; the claim is arbitrable, and non-compliance with a ruling permits proportionate counter-measures including **suspension of all or parts of the Protocol** (Joint instrument, paras 12–13; Withdrawal Agreement, Art. 178(2); AG opinion, para 9).
- **Unilateral declaration:** records the UK's position that, if replacement talks collapse through an EU breach of good faith, the UK may take measures ultimately to **disapply** the Protocol via the treaty's dispute procedures; the EU indicated it would not object (Unilateral declaration, 11 Mar 2019; AG opinion, paras 12–13).
- **The Attorney General's conclusion:** the instruments "reduce the risk" of the UK being held in the Protocol **insofar as that came about through the EU's bad faith**; but "the legal risk remains unchanged" that, through "intractable differences" alone, the UK "would have… no internationally lawful means of exiting the Protocol's arrangements, save by agreement" (Attorney General's legal opinion, 12 Mar 2019, paras 17 and 19).
- The underlying treaty terms in the package: settlement estimated at **£35–39 billion**; transition to **31 December 2020**, extendable once by joint decision before 1 July 2020; citizens' residence and work rights preserved; backstop = a single EU–UK customs territory with Northern Ireland additionally aligned on goods, terminable only by joint decision (Withdrawal Agreement, 25 Nov 2018, Arts. 126–132, Part Two; Protocol, Arts. 6 and 20).
cards.deep_lectura:
**Analyst read** *(inference — not stated verbatim in the record)*
- The package's weight rests on a legal distinction most voters never meet: interpretation versus amendment. The treaty text is untouched; the instruments harden how an arbitrator must read it. That is real in a tribunal and invisible on the page — maximum legal substance for minimum visible concession, which is precisely what made it negotiable in Strasbourg.
- Every new enforcement tooth bites only on **bad faith** — a deliberately high bar in international law. The likeliest failure mode, an honest deadlock over genuinely hard trade-offs, is exactly the scenario the instruments cannot reach, and the Attorney General's paragraph 19 says so in terms.
- "Alternative arrangements by December 2020" is a commitment to effort, not outcome: the frictionless-border technology it gestures at did not operate at scale on any customs border in the world at the time of signing.
- The unilateral declaration is diplomacy's comfort blanket: a statement of the UK's own position that the EU merely agreed not to contradict. It shifts litigation posture, not the exit key.

cards.title: Main motion, as amended by amendment (a), on UK's withdrawal from the European Union
cards.proposed_by: Government motion amended by Dame Caroline Spelman / Jack Dromey (cross-party)
cards.headline: Reject leaving the EU without a deal, in any circumstances — a formal declaration that does not change the law: exit stays set for 29 March unless a deal or a delay is agreed.
cards.source_brief:
Sixteen days before the UK is due to leave the EU, this puts the House on record that a no-deal exit must never happen — not on 29 March, not ever. The catch is in the small print: this is a declaration, not a law. Exit day is written into statute, and a resolution of the House cannot move it.

- **What "no deal" means in practice:** overnight, UK–EU trade drops onto basic **WTO terms** — border taxes both ways (**10%** on cars into the EU, over **40%** on lamb), customs checks at Dover–Calais, **no transition period**, and citizens' rights resting on each country's goodwill instead of a treaty.
- **What a vote for actually does:** it states a position. The law still says the UK leaves on **29 March, deal or no deal** — only a ratified agreement or a delay to the exit countdown changes that. This vote, by itself, changes nothing.
- **The case for:** taking the cliff edge off the table as deliberate policy — a clear signal to businesses stockpiling parts and to 3 million-plus EU residents that the crash-out is not the plan.
- **The case against:** a negotiator who has sworn never to walk away takes whatever terms are offered — ruling out no-deal hands Brussels the leverage; and a declaration that contradicts the statute book muddies who actually decides.
cards.deep_facts:
- The original Government motion declined to approve leaving without a deal **on 29 March 2019** specifically, and noted that leaving without a deal "remains the default in UK and EU law unless this House and the EU ratify an agreement". Amendment (a) struck the date and the default clause, leaving a blanket text: the House "rejects the United Kingdom leaving the European Union without a Withdrawal Agreement and a Framework for the Future Relationship" (Hansard, 13 Mar 2019).
- Resolutions of the House express its view but do not amend statute. Exit day — **11pm, 29 March 2019** — stood in the EU (Withdrawal) Act 2018 and in EU law under the two-year exit countdown of Article 50, movable only by a ratified withdrawal agreement or an extension agreed **unanimously by the 27 other EU governments** (Commons Library, CBP-8496).
- Without a deal, UK–EU trade reverts to WTO most-favoured-nation terms: EU tariffs of **10%** on finished cars and an effective **40%+** on sheep meat, a sector sending ~**95%** of its exports to the EU (AHDB, 2019).
- The Government's no-deal contingency tariff, published the same day, would make **87%** of UK imports by value tariff-free for up to 12 months, with finished cars at **10.6%** (gov.uk, 13 Mar 2019).
- Dover handles ~**10,000 lorries a day**; EU lorries clear in about **2 minutes** each. The port estimated that adding 2 minutes' processing per vehicle could produce queues of up to **17 miles** on both sides of the Channel (Port of Dover evidence to Parliament, 2018–19).
- The negotiated deal included a standstill **transition to 31 December 2020** during which rules stay unchanged; with no deal there is no transition — third-country status applies overnight (Institute for Government, 2019).
cards.deep_lectura:
**Analyst read** *(inference — not stated verbatim in the record)*
- Deleting the date is the whole game: the amendment converts a one-night reassurance about 29 March into a standing doctrine binding every future deadline — which is precisely why it is fought harder than the original wording.
- A declaratory motion's force is political, not legal: it tells the Government what the House will and will not tolerate, and, if carried, dares ministers to drive towards an outcome the elected chamber has formally rejected.
- The deeper tension is constitutional — a House steering by resolution while the statute book points the other way. Whoever relies on this vote alone is relying on convention holding under the highest pressure in the building's modern history.

cards.title: UK's withdrawal from the EU: Prime Minister's motion
cards.headline: Instruct the Government to ask the EU to delay Brexit beyond 29 March 2019 — to 30 June if a deal is approved by 20 March; any longer delay means the UK holds European Parliament elections in May.
cards.source_brief:
Exit day — 29 March 2019, written into law — is fifteen days away. This sends the Government to Brussels to ask for more time. The catch: the UK cannot grant itself a delay. All **27 other EU governments** must agree, unanimously — any one capital can say no or attach a price.

- **Two flavours of delay:** a short technical one to **30 June**, on offer only if a divorce deal is approved by **20 March** (time to pass the exit paperwork); anything longer and the UK must elect members of the European Parliament in May — **three years after voting to leave**.
- **A vote for** buys breathing room: with the deal, the laws and the border systems all unfinished, more time is the difference between leaving by design and crashing out by accident.
- **A vote against** holds the date the Government has repeated for two years: a deadline is the only force that makes anyone compromise, and a delay just moves the cliff while handing control of the timetable to 27 other capitals.
- Either way, this only **asks** — what comes back from Brussels, and with what conditions attached, is not in the House's hands.
cards.deep_facts:
- The motion commits the Government to "seek to agree with the European Union an extension of the period specified in Article 50(3)" — the EU treaty's two-year exit countdown, running since 29 March 2017 (Hansard, 14 Mar 2019).
- Its first branch: if the House approves the negotiated withdrawal agreement and future-relationship framework by **20 March 2019**, the Government seeks a **one-off extension to 30 June 2019** "for the purpose of passing the necessary EU exit legislation" (Hansard, 14 Mar 2019).
- Its second branch notes that otherwise the European Council would "require a clear purpose for any extension" and that any extension beyond 30 June **requires the UK to hold European Parliament elections in May 2019** (Hansard, 14 Mar 2019).
- Under Article 50(3) TEU, membership ends two years after notification "unless the European Council, in agreement with the Member State concerned, **unanimously** decides to extend this period" (Treaty on European Union, Art. 50).
- European Parliament elections were scheduled across the EU for **23–26 May 2019**; a state still a member at that point is legally required to elect MEPs (Commons Library, CBP-8496).
- Exit day in domestic law sat in the EU (Withdrawal) Act 2018 and could be amended by statutory instrument to match any new date agreed with the EU (Commons Library, CBP-8496).
- The next scheduled European Council summit — the last before exit day — was **21–22 March 2019** (European Council calendar).
cards.deep_lectura:
**Analyst read** *(inference — not stated verbatim in the record)*
- The two-branch design points the pressure back at the House: the only clean, short delay on offer is conditional on approving the deal within six days — extension as a lever for the deal, not an escape from it.
- Asking for time is also surrendering the timetable: once the request is made, 27 governments each hold a veto and can price their consent, and the UK's deadline stops being its own.
- The European-elections clause is the built-in poison pill — it makes any long delay carry a visible, campaignable cost, which disciplines how much time anyone dares request.

cards.title: Mr Baron's motion B (No deal)
cards.headline: Leave the EU without a deal on 12 April 2019 — a fixed exit date sixteen days away, trading on basic WTO terms from day one, with no transition period.
cards.source_brief:
The clean-break option, stated plainly: name the date and go. Under the EU's March decision, **12 April** is the default exit date unless the UK presents a way forward — this motion makes that date the destination, chosen on purpose rather than arrived at by accident.

- **What changes overnight:** UK–EU trade drops onto **WTO terms** — border taxes both ways (**10%** on cars into the EU, over **40%** on lamb), customs checks at Dover–Calais where an EU lorry clears today in about **2 minutes**, and EU-wide rules on flights, medicines and data replaced by patchwork contingency measures.
- **What a vote for buys:** certainty and an end — no more extensions, no European elections three years after the referendum, no exit terms set by Brussels; the future trade relationship gets negotiated afterwards, from outside.
- **What it costs:** the **£39 billion** divorce settlement agreed in the negotiated deal goes back into dispute, and more than **3 million** EU citizens in the UK plus around **1 million** Britons in the EU swap treaty protection for each country's own goodwill scheme.
- There is **no transition**: the negotiated deal kept rules unchanged until end-2020 to let people and firms adapt; this route has day one arrive with no runway.
cards.deep_facts:
- The motion's text: "That this House agrees that the UK shall leave the EU on 12 April 2019 without a deal" (Hansard, 27 Mar 2019).
- The date comes from the European Council decision of 22 March 2019, which moved exit day off 29 March: **22 May 2019** if the House approves the withdrawal agreement, otherwise **12 April 2019**, by when the UK "will indicate a way forward" for the Council to consider (European Council decision, 22 Mar 2019).
- On WTO terms the EU applies its standard external tariff to UK goods: **10%** on finished cars; an effective **40%+** on sheep meat, a sector sending ~**95%** of its exports to the EU (AHDB, 2019). The UK's announced contingency tariff would make **87%** of imports by value tariff-free for up to 12 months (gov.uk, 13 Mar 2019).
- Dover handles ~**10,000 lorries a day**; the port estimated that adding **2 minutes'** processing per vehicle could produce queues of up to **17 miles** on both sides of the Channel (Port of Dover evidence to Parliament, 2018–19).
- The negotiated deal included a standstill **transition to 31 December 2020**; without a deal there is none — the EU's published no-deal contingency measures (e.g. basic flight connectivity, time-limited haulage access) are unilateral, temporary and revocable (European Commission contingency notices, 2019).
- The vote was recorded on **signed ballot papers** handed in by each MP rather than by walking the division lobbies, with results announced later the same evening (Hansard, 27 Mar 2019).
cards.deep_lectura:
**Analyst read** *(inference — not stated verbatim in the record)*
- Naming the date is the point: turning no-deal from a default that happens to you into a destination you chose changes the negotiation — nothing concentrates minds in Brussels like a counterpart demonstrably prepared to walk.
- The same choice spends the UK's remaining time without a plan for the morning after: the cushioning on the EU side is unilateral and revocable, so the leverage gained at the table is borrowed against the days right after leaving it.
- The certainty on offer is certainty about the date, not the terms — everything that matters about the future relationship would still have to be negotiated, from outside, with the same counterpart and less to trade.

cards.title: George Eustice's motion H (EFTA and EEA)
cards.headline: Keep Britain inside Europe's single market as a non-EU member, Norway-style: people, services and capital keep moving freely, but the UK leaves the EU's tariff club so it can set its own tariffs and sign its own trade deals.
cards.source_brief:
The Norway arrangement: leave the EU but stay in its single market — the giant shared marketplace — by rejoining EFTA, the small club of non-EU countries (Norway, Iceland, Liechtenstein) that trade inside it. Day-to-day business with Europe carries on much as now. The twist: this plan deliberately stays OUT of the EU's tariff club, so Britain gets its trade policy back — and pays for it at the border.

- **What Britain gets back:** tariffs and trade deals. Outside the EU's tariff club, the UK sets its own import taxes and can sign its own deals with America, India, anyone.
- **The price at the border:** exporters to Europe would face customs paperwork proving where their goods were made, and farm-and-food trade — including across the Irish border — needs a separate fix this plan only promises to negotiate.
- **The price at home:** free movement continues — EU citizens keep the right to live and work in the UK — and Britain keeps paying into the club and following the market rulebook without a vote on it.
cards.deep_facts:
- The motion instructs the Government to: (a) assert the UK's existing rights as a signatory to the EEA agreement; (b) make EEA rights and obligations operable through the domestic courts on an emergency basis; (c) apply to rejoin EFTA at the earliest opportunity; and (d) decline to enter a customs union with the EU, while seeking new protocols on the Northern Ireland border and agri-food trade [Hansard, EU: Withdrawal and Future Relationship (Votes), Motion (H), 27 Mar 2019].
- The EEA agreement extends the single market's four freedoms — goods, services, capital and persons — to the three non-EU EFTA states (Norway, Iceland, Liechtenstein); free movement of people is part of the package [EFTA / EEA agreement].
- Non-EU EEA states adopt single-market legislation without a vote in the EU's law-making institutions and make financial contributions (in Norway's case via the EEA and Norway Grants and programme payments) [House of Commons Library; EFTA].
- EFTA states are outside the EU customs union: they run independent trade policies and their own network of free-trade agreements, and their exports to the EU are subject to customs formalities and rules-of-origin requirements [EFTA; Institute for Government].
- The EEA agreement does not cover the EU's common agricultural and fisheries policies or customs — which is why the motion seeks separate protocols for agri-food trade and the Northern Ireland border [EFTA; Hansard motion text].
- Put to the House on 27 March 2019 as a recorded (deferred-style) division under the backbench-controlled process established by the business motion of that day [CommonsVotes, division 657].
cards.deep_lectura: **Analyst read** *(inference — not stated verbatim in the record)*: this is the softest exit that still returns an independent trade policy — pitched at leavers who care about trade sovereignty and remainers who care about the economy. Its two exposed flanks are the two things it does not change: free movement, the most legible message of the referendum, continues untouched; and by refusing the tariff club it re-creates a customs problem — including in Ireland — that the text answers only with a promise of future 'protocols'. Whether it reads as the best of both worlds or the worst — paying and obeying a rulebook with no vote, while still queuing at customs — depends on which referendum promise the reader weights.

cards.title: Jeremy Corbyn's motion K (Labour's alternative plan)
cards.headline: Order the Government to renegotiate Brexit so the UK stays in a permanent customs union with the EU, aligns closely with the single market, and keeps rights and standards automatically in step with Europe's — with those objectives locked into law.
cards.source_brief:
The full alternative to the exit package on the Government's table: leave the EU's political institutions but stay economically tied to them, and make that the legally binding goal of the talks.

- **Customs union, permanent:** no tariffs and no customs checks on goods with the EU — but one shared tariff wall, so no independent UK trade deals on goods. It demands 'a UK say' in future EU trade deals, something the EU has never granted a non-member.
- **Dynamic alignment:** UK rights and workplace standards would update automatically as the EU's do. Protections can't fall behind Europe's — and the rules are written in Brussels, where the UK would no longer have ministers or MEPs voting.
- **Locked in:** the objectives would be put into an Act of Parliament, binding whoever is negotiating.
- **The stake:** for — frictionless trade for factories and farms and a soft landing for jobs; against — the UK keeps the EU's rulebook and tariff wall while giving up its vote on both, and loses the free hand on trade that was a core argument for leaving.
cards.deep_facts:
- The motion required ministers to negotiate changes to the draft Withdrawal Agreement and Political Declaration to secure five objectives: (i) a permanent UK–EU customs union; (ii) close alignment with the single market 'underpinned by shared institutions and obligations'; (iii) dynamic alignment on rights and protections; (iv) commitments on participation in EU agencies and funding programmes, including environment, education and industrial regulation; (v) agreement on future security arrangements, including access to the European Arrest Warrant and shared databases (Hansard, 27 Mar 2019).
- A second limb required primary legislation giving those negotiating objectives statutory status (Hansard, 27 Mar 2019).
- The five objectives restate negotiating demands put to the Prime Minister in a letter of 6 February 2019 (BBC/Guardian, Feb 2019).
- A customs union means a common external tariff: members apply the same tariffs to non-members and cannot conclude independent trade agreements on goods. The existing precedent for a non-member customs union, Turkey, carries no vote in EU trade policy (Institute for Government, customs union explainer, 2019).
- 'Dynamic alignment' means domestic rules track new EU rules as they are adopted, as opposed to 'non-regression', which only sets a floor at current standards (Institute for Government, 2019).
- EU leaders had stated the Withdrawal Agreement itself was not open for renegotiation, but that the Political Declaration on the future relationship could be redrafted quickly if UK red lines changed (European Council/Tusk statements, Mar 2019).
cards.deep_lectura: **Analyst read** *(inference — not stated verbatim in the record)*: the plan keeps goods trade frictionless and thereby answers most of the Irish border question through economics rather than through the contested backstop. Its real subject is voice: tariff policy and product standards would be set in Brussels with the UK outside the room, which is why the 'UK say in future EU trade deals' clause exists — it is unprecedented for a non-member, so it functions either as a bargaining chip to be traded away or as a built-in exit ramp if talks sour. The statutory-objectives limb is the sharper instrument: it would bind any Prime Minister — current or future — to this destination by Act of Parliament, shifting control of the negotiation's endpoint from Government to the Commons.
cards.raw_outcome: Jeremy Corbyn's motion K (Labour's alternative plan)

cards.title: Joanna Cherry's motion L (Revocation to avoid no deal)
cards.headline: Cancel Brexit rather than leave with no deal: if no exit deal is law two sitting days before exit day and Parliament refuses to approve leaving without one, the Government must revoke Article 50 — and the UK stays in the EU on its existing terms.
cards.source_brief:
A legal safety-catch against crashing out. The EU's top court ruled in December 2018 that the UK can cancel its leave notice on its own — no permission from the other 27 needed, membership terms unchanged. This motion turns that power into the default at the cliff edge.

- **The trigger:** it only fires at the brink — if, two sitting days before exit day, no withdrawal deal has been passed into law.
- **One last vote:** MPs would be asked point-blank to approve a no-deal exit. Approve it, and the UK leaves without a deal as planned.
- **Refuse it, and Brexit is cancelled** — not paused. The court ruled revocation must be unequivocal and unconditional: the UK stays in on its current terms, rebate and opt-outs intact, and can't legally use it as a trick to buy negotiating time.
- **The stake:** for — insurance that a no-deal exit can only ever happen if a majority of MPs actively chooses it; against — it lets Parliament cancel EU withdrawal at the last minute without asking voters first, and strips the UK's walk-away threat from every future negotiation moment.
cards.deep_facts:
- The motion provided that if, on the day before the end of the penultimate Commons sitting day before exit day, no Act of Parliament had been passed approving a withdrawal agreement (for the purposes of section 13(1)(d) of the EU (Withdrawal) Act 2018), the Government 'must immediately put a motion to the House asking it to approve No Deal'; if the House withheld approval, the Government 'must ensure' the Article 50 notice was revoked in accordance with UK and EU law (Hansard, 27 Mar 2019).
- The Court of Justice of the EU ruled in Wightman (Case C-621/18, 10 Dec 2018) that a member state may unilaterally revoke its Article 50 notification, provided the withdrawal agreement has not entered into force and the negotiating period has not expired, and the revocation follows a democratic process under national constitutional requirements (CJEU press release 191/18, 10 Dec 2018).
- The same ruling requires revocation to be 'unequivocal and unconditional': it confirms EU membership on unchanged terms and brings the withdrawal procedure to an end (CJEU, C-621/18).
- The case was brought by a group of Scottish parliamentarians and referred by the Court of Session in Edinburgh (CJEU, C-621/18).
- At the time of the vote, exit day stood at 12 April 2019 if the negotiated Withdrawal Agreement was not approved, or 22 May 2019 if it was (European Council decision, 22 Mar 2019).
- The motion was an instruction to Government, not legislation: revocation itself would still have required Government action (and, on one reading of the Gina Miller precedent, statutory authority) under UK constitutional law (Commons Library, Article 50 briefings, 2019).
cards.deep_lectura: **Analyst read** *(inference — not stated verbatim in the record)*: this is the only mechanism that takes a no-deal exit off the table without depending on EU goodwill over extensions — everything else at the brink needed the other 27 to agree. Its design also redistributes blame: nobody has to propose cancelling Brexit; cancellation simply happens unless a majority puts its name to no-deal, which is precisely the vote most MPs least wanted to own. The deeper effect is on bargaining: once revocation is the automatic fallback, the threat of crashing out stops pressuring anyone into supporting a negotiated deal. Critics noted a legal tension — if revocation were intended as a staging post before re-triggering Article 50, it would collide with the court's 'unequivocal and unconditional' condition (InFacts, Mar 2019), so the motion only works honestly as a genuine stay-in.
cards.raw_outcome: Joanna Cherry's motion L (Revocation to avoid no deal)

cards.title: Mr Fysh's motion O (Contingent preferential arrangements)
cards.headline: Leave the EU without the negotiated deal and seek a bare-bones standby instead: ask Brussels to agree zero tariffs on all goods and frozen standards for up to two years under world-trade rules, while a full trade deal is worked out.
cards.source_brief:
The managed no-deal option: walk away from the negotiated package — backstop, exit terms and all — but immediately offer the EU a skeleton arrangement so trade doesn't hit a wall on day one.

- **What's offered:** tariff-free, quota-free trade in all goods plus mutual recognition of standards, each for up to two years — and the UK keeps paying Brussels roughly its current net contribution while the standby runs.
- **The legal small print:** the world-trade rule invoked (GATT Article XXIV) only covers interim agreements that **both sides sign** on the way to a full trade deal. No EU signature, no standstill — it cannot be triggered unilaterally.
- **And Brussels had said no:** the EU's stated position was that after a no-deal exit there would be no trade talks until the exit bill, citizens' rights and the Irish border were settled — and that its standard tariffs (10% on cars, far higher on much food) would apply in the meantime.
- **The stake:** for — out on time, free of the negotiated terms, with a credible-sounding offer that tests whether EU commercial interest beats its rulebook; against — the whole plan needs the other side's consent, and if that consent never comes the standby never starts: full tariffs from day one.
cards.deep_facts:
- The motion directed that, if the UK were 'unable to implement a Withdrawal Agreement with the EU', the Government should seek to agree with the EU: (a) a trade agreement and/or joint notification of trade preference covering 100% of goods traded, with no tariffs or quantitative restrictions and full cumulation of rules of origin, for up to two years; (b) a standstill of mutual recognition of standards and conformity assessment for up to two years, with the UK complying with the EU legislative acquis as retained on exit day; (c) customs arrangements using simplified procedures performed away from UK/EU borders; and (d) payments to the EU equivalent to the UK's current net annual contribution for up to two years in respect of those arrangements (Hansard, 27 Mar 2019).
- GATT Article XXIV permits departures from most-favoured-nation tariff rules for free-trade areas and customs unions, including 'interim agreements' leading to one — but an interim agreement must be concluded by the parties and include a plan and schedule for the final agreement within a reasonable length of time; it cannot be invoked by one side alone (House of Commons Library, 'No-deal Brexit and WTO: Article 24 explained', 2019; Full Fact, 2019).
- Without such an agreement, WTO most-favoured-nation rules would oblige the EU to apply its common external tariff to UK goods — 10% on cars, with substantially higher rates on many agricultural products (EU common external tariff schedule; Full Fact, 2019).
- The EU's chief negotiator had stated that after a no-deal exit the EU would not open trade negotiations until the financial settlement, citizens' rights and the Ireland/Northern Ireland border were addressed (Barnier statements, 2019); the EU trade commissioner stated UK–EU trade would proceed on most-favoured-nation terms, meaning new tariffs, until an agreement existed (Malmström, reported 2019).
- The motion's only border provision was clause (c)'s facilitation — declarations and controls performed away from the border; it proposed no specific arrangement for the Irish land border beyond that (Hansard, 27 Mar 2019).
cards.deep_lectura: **Analyst read** *(inference — not stated verbatim in the record)*: the motion's real wager is that once the UK had actually left, EU commercial self-interest would override its stated sequencing — that a tariff wall hurting both sides would force Brussels to sign the standstill it had refused to discuss. The drafting quietly concedes the legal point its supporters often blurred in public: 'joint notification' admits GATT XXIV needs two signatures, and clause (d)'s continued payments — roughly the current net contribution, without calling it an exit bill — is the sweetener meant to buy that second signature. The unaddressed risk is asymmetric: if the EU held its line, the standby never begins and the outcome is indistinguishable from an unmanaged no-deal exit, with the offer having cost nothing to refuse.
cards.raw_outcome: Mr Fysh's motion O (Contingent preferential arrangements)

cards.title: United Kingdom's withdrawal from the European Union
cards.headline: Approve the EU divorce treaty on its own — the £39 billion settlement, citizens' rights, the standstill to end-2020 and the customs backstop — setting aside the future-relationship declaration for a separate decision, and locking in an orderly exit on 22 May 2019.
cards.source_brief:
Decided on the very day the UK was originally due to leave the EU. The treaty is split from its companion paper: on the table are only the binding divorce terms, not the non-binding declaration about the future relationship. The EU's standing offer makes today a hard deadline — approve the treaty by tonight and exit day moves to **22 May** with a deal; fail, and the legal default becomes **12 April**, two weeks away, with nothing agreed.

- **What's in scope:** the binding terms only — about **£39 billion** settled, rights for **3 million+** EU citizens in the UK and **~1 million** Britons in the EU, business rules frozen to **end-2020**, and the backstop keeping the UK in EU customs rules until both sides agree a replacement.
- **What's set aside:** the declaration sketching future trade, security and fishing. Approving this motion does **not** ratify the treaty by itself — the law still requires a separate approval of that declaration, plus legislation, before ratification.
- **The clock:** under the EU's 22 March decision, approval today buys an orderly runway to **22 May**; without it, the choices shrink to a 12 April cliff edge, or asking for a long delay that obliges the UK to hold **European Parliament elections** three years after voting to leave.
- **The handle:** bank the orderly exit now and fight about the future afterwards — or refuse to sign half a package when the half being signed contains its hardest clause, the backstop, and the £39 billion.
cards.deep_facts:
- The motion asks the House to approve the **withdrawal agreement only**, decoupled from the Political Declaration — the non-binding outline of the future relationship (Hansard, 29 Mar 2019).
- It notes the **European Council Decision of 22 March 2019**, agreed with the UK: the Article 50 period (the formal two-year exit countdown) extends to **22 May 2019** only if the Commons approves the withdrawal agreement **by 29 March 2019**; otherwise it runs to **12 April 2019**; any extension beyond 22 May would require the UK to hold **European Parliament elections** (European Council Decision (EU) 2019/476, 22 Mar 2019; Hansard, 29 Mar 2019).
- Approval of this motion would **not** meet section 13(1)(b) of the EU (Withdrawal) Act 2018, which requires the Commons to approve both the agreement **and** the future-relationship framework before ratification; the Government brought it forward to satisfy the European Council's condition, with ratification still needing the further statutory approvals and implementing legislation (EU (Withdrawal) Act 2018; Commons Library CDP-2019-0079).
- **29 March 2019** had been exit day in domestic law — two years from the Article 50 notification — until regulations made under the 2018 Act redefined it that week in line with the European Council decision (EU (Withdrawal) Act 2018, s20; exit-day amendment regulations, Mar 2019).
- The House sat on a **Friday** — not a normal sitting day — so the decision could be taken within the European Council's deadline (Hansard, 29 Mar 2019).
- The treaty being approved: financial settlement estimated at **£35–39 billion**; citizens' residence, work and healthcare rights, with permanent status after **five years'** residence; transition to **31 December 2020**, extendable once by joint decision before 1 July 2020; the Protocol on Ireland/Northern Ireland — a single EU–UK customs territory with Northern Ireland additionally aligned to single-market rules for goods, terminable only by **joint** UK–EU decision that it is "no longer necessary" (Withdrawal Agreement, 25 Nov 2018, Arts. 126–132, Part Two; Protocol, Arts. 6 and 20).
- The Attorney General's published advice on the Protocol: in international law it "would endure indefinitely" until superseded by agreement (Attorney General's advice, 13 Nov 2018).
cards.deep_lectura:
**Analyst read** *(inference — not stated verbatim in the record)*
- Splitting the treaty from the declaration converts a treaty question into a deadline question: the substance is identical either way, but the vote is engineered around the EU's calendar — six more orderly weeks ride on a single sitting day.
- Legally, little is lost by deferring the declaration — it was never enforceable. Politically, everything is visible: approving the binding half alone makes 'pay £39 billion with the future left blank' literal rather than rhetorical.
- The choreography concedes where leverage lives: a chamber voting under a two-week cliff edge is being asked to price catastrophe, not the treaty. Whether that pressure reads as statesmanship or as coercion is itself the fault line the motion stands on.
- Holding European Parliament elections three years after the referendum is the scenario every side claims to want least — which makes it the silent third option doing most of the work in this decision.
cards.raw_outcome: United Kingdom's withdrawal from the European Union

cards.title: Mr Clarke's motion C (Customs Union)
cards.headline: Write into law that any Brexit deal must keep the whole UK in a permanent customs union with the EU: goods keep crossing tariff-free in both directions, but Britain gives up signing its own trade deals on goods.
cards.source_brief:
A customs union is the EU's tariff club: members charge the rest of the world the same import taxes and charge each other nothing. This plan would bind the Government — in an Act of Parliament, not just a negotiating aim — to keep Britain in such a club with the EU, permanently and for the whole UK. It is the minimum-change option: it fixes the factory floor and the border, and touches nothing else.

- **What it fixes:** no tariffs on goods either way and no tariff checks at Dover or on the Irish border — cross-Channel supply chains in cars, food and medicines keep working as today.
- **What it costs:** an independent trade policy. Britain would apply the EU's tariff at its own borders and could not undercut it in deals with the US, India or anyone else — goods would be off the table in every future negotiation.
- **What it doesn't touch:** services (around 80% of the UK economy), immigration and the market rulebook. EU free movement is not kept by this plan, and there are no membership payments.
- **Permanent means permanent:** putting it in primary legislation ties the hands of future governments, not just this one.
cards.deep_facts:
- The motion instructs the Government to: (1) ensure that any Withdrawal Agreement and Political Declaration negotiated with the EU includes, as a minimum, a commitment to negotiate a permanent and comprehensive UK-wide customs union with the EU; and (2) enshrine this objective in primary legislation [Hansard, EU Withdrawal and Future Relationship (Votes), Motion (C), 1 Apr 2019].
- In a customs union, members apply a common external tariff and goods circulate between them tariff-free; a member cannot set lower tariffs of its own or conclude separate trade agreements on goods tariffs [Institute for Government, customs union explainer].
- A customs union removes tariffs and rules-of-origin checks but not regulatory checks: on its own it does not eliminate all border controls on goods, and it does not cover trade in services [Institute for Government; House of Commons Library].
- Customs-union membership entails neither free movement of people, nor single-market membership, nor EU budget contributions; the EU–Turkey customs union, for example, covers industrial goods and processed agricultural products only [House of Commons Library].
- The 'UK-wide' wording specifies a single customs territory covering Great Britain and Northern Ireland alike [Hansard motion text].
- Put to the House on 1 April 2019 as a recorded division under the backbench-controlled process established by the business motion of that day [CommonsVotes, division 666].
cards.deep_lectura: **Analyst read** *(inference — not stated verbatim in the record)*: the minimalist soft Brexit, engineered to be the easiest thing for a divided House to swallow — it honours the headline referendum result (out of the EU, free movement not retained, no payments in) while keeping manufacturers' supply lines and the Irish land border intact. The give-away is trade policy: 'permanent' means Britain applies a tariff set in Brussels indefinitely without a vote on it, and the demand for primary legislation is the real teeth — it is designed to bind future ministers, not merely steer one negotiation. What it conspicuously does not buy is frictionless trade: regulatory checks, and the services economy, are left for another day.

verification.motion_text: Full text verified via TheyWorkForYou, 'Motion (C) Customs Union', 1 Apr 2019 (theyworkforyou.com/debates/?id=2019-04-01b.893.2): 'That this House instructs the Government to (1) ensure that any Withdrawal Agreement and Political Declaration negotiated with the EU must include, as a minimum, a commitment to negotiate a permanent and comprehensive UK-wide customs union with the EU; (2) enshrine this objective in primary legislation.'

The SNP abstained on the customs-union-only option in BOTH indicative rounds (27 Mar Motion J and 1 Apr Motion C); the 3 SNP members beyond the whipped abstention were reported absent for personal reasons. cards.title: Nick Boles's motion D (Common Market 2.0)
cards.headline: Stay in both of Europe's economic clubs after leaving the EU — the single market, with free movement of people, plus a full customs arrangement — so goods, services and people keep moving as they do today while Britain exits the EU's political institutions.
cards.source_brief:
'Common Market 2.0': the closest you can get to the EU without being a member — a return, the pitch goes, to the common market Britain joined in 1973. The UK would rejoin EFTA, the small club of non-EU countries (Norway, Iceland, Liechtenstein) that trade inside the single market, AND bolt on a customs arrangement so goods cross borders with no tariffs and no paperwork. Norway's deal, plus the tariff club Norway itself stays out of.

- **Almost nothing changes at the border:** no tariffs, no customs queues, no hard border in Ireland — trade in goods and services carries on essentially as now.
- **What Britain gives up:** its own trade deals. It would apply the EU's external tariff with a promised 'say' — not a vote — on future EU trade deals, follow the market rulebook it no longer writes, and keep paying in, as Norway does.
- **Free movement continues** — EU citizens keep the right to live and work in the UK. Supporters lean on a treaty 'emergency brake' on migration that Norway has never used.
- **What's actually left:** the EU's political project — no more MEPs, and out of the EU's farm and fisheries policies.
cards.deep_facts:
- The motion instructs the Government to renegotiate the Political Declaration so that the UK: accedes to EFTA, having negotiated a derogation from Article 56(3) of the EFTA convention to allow participation in a customs arrangement with the EU; joins the EFTA pillar of the EEA, continuing single-market participation; agrees protocols on frictionless agri-food trade across the UK/EU border; and enters a comprehensive customs arrangement including a common external tariff, alignment with the Union Customs Code and an agreement on commercial policy including a UK say on future EU trade deals — at least until alternative arrangements maintaining frictionless trade and no hard border in Ireland are agreed [Hansard, EU Withdrawal and Future Relationship (Votes), Motion (D), 1 Apr 2019].
- EEA participation entails the single market's four freedoms, including free movement of persons; non-EU EEA states adopt single-market legislation without a vote in EU institutions and make financial contributions [EFTA / EEA agreement; House of Commons Library].
- The customs add-on is what separates this from Norway's actual position: Norway is outside the EU customs union and runs an independent trade policy; under a common external tariff the UK could not [efta-studies.org; Institute for Government].
- Article 112 of the EEA agreement (the safeguard clause) permits unilateral measures where serious economic or societal difficulties arise; it has been invoked by Liechtenstein to limit migration but never by Norway [EEA agreement; House of Commons Library].
- The EEA agreement does not cover the EU's common agricultural and fisheries policies — hence the motion's separate agri-food protocols [EFTA; Hansard motion text].
- Put to the House on 1 April 2019 as a recorded division under the backbench-controlled process established by the business motion of that day [CommonsVotes, division 667].
cards.deep_lectura: **Analyst read** *(inference — not stated verbatim in the record)*: built as the compromise a hung Parliament might actually pass — economically soft enough for remainers (market intact, Irish border open) and dressed in enough exit (out of the political institutions, out of farm-and-fish policy) to be sold as honouring the referendum. The cost is candour: Britain would obey market rules it no longer writes, pay to do so, apply a tariff it does not set, and keep free movement — with a treaty clause never tested by Norway as the only answer on immigration. The 'at least until alternative arrangements' wording quietly concedes the customs bolt-on could become permanent. It trades sovereignty on paper for continuity in fact; readers who think 2016 was about control will find the deal-breaker exactly where supporters find the selling point.

verification.motion_text: Full text verified via the Order Paper for 1 April 2019 (publications.parliament.uk, 'Business for Monday 01 April 2019') and contemporaneous reproductions (ConservativeHome, LabourList): EFTA accession with Art. 56(3) derogation, EEA EFTA-pillar entry, agri-food protocols, comprehensive customs arrangement with common external tariff, Union Customs Code alignment and a UK say on future EU trade deals, at least until alternative arrangements keep trade frictionless and the Irish border open.

cards.title: Peter Kyle's motion E (Confirmatory public vote)
cards.headline: Require a confirmatory public vote on the exit deal: whatever withdrawal package Parliament passes cannot be implemented or ratified until voters have approved it in a referendum.
cards.source_brief:
Not a vote on any particular deal — a lock on every deal. Parliament could still pass whatever withdrawal package it likes; this motion says none of it takes effect until the public has approved the actual signed terms directly.

- **What changes:** ratifying the exit deal currently needs Parliament alone. This adds a second key, held by voters — approval of the concrete deal on paper, not the idea of leaving in general.
- **What it doesn't settle:** the motion sets no question, no date and no alternative option. A referendum needs its own Act of Parliament, an independently tested question, and roughly **22 weeks minimum** to organise — which means a long extension of EU membership first.
- **The stake:** for — a change this permanent gets checked against its real, final terms before it becomes irreversible, and a deal that survives that check gains legitimacy no parliamentary majority can give it; against — months more uncertainty for households and business, and a deal could pass Parliament yet die at the ballot box, leaving the country with no agreed path at all.
cards.deep_facts:
- The motion provided that the House would not allow, in that Parliament, the implementation and ratification of any withdrawal agreement and any framework for the future relationship unless and until they had been approved by the people of the United Kingdom in a confirmatory public vote (Hansard, 1 Apr 2019).
- It applied to any withdrawal deal Parliament might approve, not to a specific package (Hansard, 1 Apr 2019).
- The motion was indicative, not legislative: holding a referendum in the UK requires primary legislation, and the Electoral Commission must assess the intelligibility and neutrality of the proposed question under the Political Parties, Elections and Referendums Act 2000 (Commons Library, referendum briefings).
- The UCL Constitution Unit estimated a further Brexit referendum would take about 22 weeks minimum from the introduction of legislation to polling day (UCL Constitution Unit, 'The mechanics of a further referendum on Brexit', 2018).
- At the time of the vote, exit day stood at 12 April 2019 if no withdrawal agreement was approved; a confirmatory vote would therefore have required a further Article 50 extension agreed with the EU (European Council decision, 22 Mar 2019).
- Under the EU (Withdrawal) Act 2018, ratification of a withdrawal agreement already required prior Commons approval; the motion added a public-approval stage on top of, not instead of, that parliamentary stage (EU (Withdrawal) Act 2018, s13).
cards.deep_lectura: **Analyst read** *(inference — not stated verbatim in the record)*: the design is deliberately deal-neutral — it lets MPs vote for a withdrawal package they dislike, knowing the public holds the final veto, which is why its sponsors pitched it as a way to unlock a parliamentary majority rather than as a route to any particular outcome. But the neutrality cuts both ways: opponents of a deal could wave it through expecting it to lose at the ballot box, and any negotiated package would face a campaign fought over far more than its text. The motion is silent on the ballot's alternative option, and that silence is doing work — the widely understood default was that rejecting the deal would mean remaining in the EU, which is the unstated route this mechanism keeps open without anyone having to vote for it directly.
